data.title: Republicans back Trump, Xi, Putin meeting but warn they are 'not our friends'
data.description:
Republican lawmakers are offering mixed reactions to President Trump’s warm embrace of Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Some view the theatrical trilateral as a poor signal of where U.S. priorities lie, while others defend an American leader open to having tough conversations with powerful countries. 

“I’ve never been successful in getting inside the president’s head, but I can tell you where I am, we have to be more clear about who our friends are and who our allies are,” said Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah), a member of the Senate Foreign Relations and Senate Judiciary Committee. 

“I would put neither of those in that category.” 

Alabama Gov.-elect Tommy Tuberville (R) said that Russia and China “control the world,” and Trump’s meeting with them is aimed at ending wars in Ukraine and Iran, conflicts where the U.S. is on the opposite side of Russia and China. 

“I don’t care who he meets with, we’ve got to get this over with,” Tuberville told The Hill. 

“They’re all involved in some form or fashion. So you bring all the leaders of the world together and try to work it out. I mean, I’d rather him do that than sit over here and worry about air traffic control.”

Xi gave an uncharacteristic hug to Trump upon his arrival Wednesday in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, which is hosting the leader-level conference of the Asia Pacific Economic Forum (APEC). Xi met Trump on the tarmac, a reciprocal gesture following the Chinese leader’s visit to Washington in September. 

Before the 21-member family photo of APEC leaders, Xi arranged a brief conversation with Trump and Putin. A U.S. official said Trump and Putin are expected to meet privately, in addition to the trilateral summit on Thursday. 

Russia’s war in Ukraine and the U.S. war against Iran are expected to come up, Trump previewed to reporters. China and Russia have both supported Iran, purchasing its oil, reportedly providing intelligence and maintaining trade ties, that have helped Tehran resist U.S. military and economic pressure. 

Trump said he wants to talk about denuclearization, issues that Xi has shown little appetite to engage in. The White House downplayed an agreement to come out of the meetings, a view echoed by Republicans, who were putting the blame on Xi. 

“I don’t believe any agreements are going to be made, but certainly China has resisted being part of any agreements,” Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), the chairman of the House Select Committee on U.S. competition with China, said on CBS’s Face the Nation on Sunday. 

“I think it’s important that the president meet with these leaders,” he said. 

“And if there’s a way to provide more security for the American people through those kinds of discussions, I think it’s important to have it.”

Sen. Bill Hagerty (R-Tenn.), a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, described Xi and Putin as “adversaries,” but said Trump meeting with them was a “healthy thing.” 

Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) called for Trump to be “tough” on both Xi and Putin during the trilateral meeting, pointing out concerns over allegations China recruited a spy against the former CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, and push Russia into a deal with Ukraine, in an interview with Fox News.

Banks added that “The President knows that China and Russia are not our friends though.”

Democrats, in a joint statement, warned Trump against wasting this opportunity to cozy up with Xi and Putin in the face of deep security concerns against the U.S. and its partners. 

“China and Russia are cooperating in unprecedented and dangerous ways to undermine American security and prosperity. Xi and Putin cannot be allowed to use this meeting as a forum to advance their interests at the expense of the United States,” the statement read.

“American security cannot be traded away for photo opportunities or personal aggrandizement.”

The statement was signed by Senators Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), the outgoing Ranking Member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Chris Coons (D-Del.), Tim Kaine (D-Va.), Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) and Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.).

Sen. Steve Daines (R-Mont.) pushed back on framing the summit as “Yalta.” The post-World War II meeting between President Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Russian leader Joseph Stalin at the Black Sea town of Yalta on the Crimean peninsula put forth an image of great-powers shaping the world order. 

“I don’t think it’s Yalta. If there’s a negotiated settlement, it’s going to involve [Ukrainian President] Zelensky, Putin, and President Trump, but I think there’s a lot of substantive issues that can be discussed,” he said in an interview with Fox News on Wednesday. 

Trump and Xi have the power to pressure Putin to halt the war, Zelensky told NBC News on Wednesday, pointing out both Xi and Trump’s support for Moscow through energy purchases. While China is one of Russia’s top oil importers, Trump waived sanctions on countries buying Russian energy and offered to import Russian diesel to lower costs in the U.S. 

“If China and the United States will put sanctions, or will say that they will put sanctions, stop export-import trade between Russia and these countries, that’s the end of the war,” Zelensky said.

The Ukrainian leader spoke the day after Ukraine’s military attacked the Kerch bridge connecting Russia with Ukraine’s occupied Crimean Peninsula — framing the attack as retaliatory for Russia’s attacks on its civilian energy infrastructure. Ukraine’s military said it had destroyed a section of the bridge roadway, while the bridge’s train tracks remained. 

“It’s their right to speak about anything. But if they want to decide something about Ukraine, it will be just rhetoric,” Zelensky told NBC. “The experience of this war between us showed it several times,” he said.

The strike was a major feat demonstrating the variety of Ukraine’s home-made weapons as it faces munition shortages provided by the U.S. and Europe. Zelensky said the bombardment against Kerch included its “Flamingo,” a long-range, ground-launched cruise missile. 

“We have repeatedly offered Russia steps toward de-escalation – and every proposal has been met with loud rejection,” Zelensky said in a post on X. “Russia strikes our infrastructure every day… Ukraine’s defensive capabilities are strong and will remain so, and we will never leave terror against our cities and people unanswered.”

data.title: Former cybersecurity director: Tech outages 'ultimately a good news story'
data.description:
Chris Krebs, the former director of the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, on Wednesday said that the recent spate of technology outages from the past week are “ultimately a good news story.”

“I know it kind of sucks in the moment when you can’t access your app or your flights are delayed, but we’re finding vulnerabilities,” Krebs told CNN’s Jake Tapper. “We’re finding bugs, we’re fixing them before our adversaries find them themselves and bring a network down intentionally.”

Americans have seen a wave of outages affecting businesses like Microsoft and Apple, as well as an outage that paused all internal communications at the National Security Agency (NSA). An outage likely caused by a router at a radio facility in Arkansas prompted the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to issue a nationwide ground stop of all flights, the third in the last 25 years.

Krebs said he agreed with Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who both said there was no evidence suggesting these outages were caused by cyberattacks.

“If it was the Chinese, they’d either burn that network to the ground or they’d be in there,” Krebs told Tapper. “You’d never know they were there. So cyberattacks tend to be either very visible or very stealthy, not this muddy middle area.”

Outages that affected the FAA and Apple occurred amid updates or upgrades to their software. Krebs said that companies using frontier AI models from tech companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have those models find bugs and patch them.

He also emphasized how it’s “human nature to string things together” regarding the frequency of these outages, but said “it’s a coincidence.”

Krebs said he expects to see more outages in the future but said “we just kind of need to take a breath, take a beat and realize that it’s not the end of the world,” noting how these recent outages lasted mere hours and not several days.

Tapper noted how people have stockpiled food and water in response to these incidents, and asked Krebs what he tells them. He replied that emergency plans should always be in place, whether in preparation for a wildfire in Los Angeles, a hurricane in Florida, a tornado in the Midwest or a winter storm in the Midatlantic and Northeast.

President Trump ousted Krebs from his previous role after affirming that 2020 election, where Trump lost reelection, was secure.

The rash of outages and digital disruptions over the past week have raised questions about potential vulnerabilities to large-scale cybersecurity. Mullin suggested it could have been caused by super intelligence (SI), the Trump administration’s preferred term for artificial intelligence.

But lawmakers have questioned the coincidence of these disruptions, with some Republicans urging Trump to address Americans at how the White House will respond.

Trump told reporters Tuesday that “it’s fine” when it comes to this incidents, adding that “things like that happen.”

data.title: Top Republican says $350 billion defense reconciliation topline is 'not gonna happen'
data.description:
Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Ala.), the chairman of the House Armed Services Committee (HASC), poured cold water on Wednesday on the Pentagon’s $350 billion defense reconciliation topline ask during a Hudson Institute event in Washington, D.C. on Wednesday.

“By the way, [$]350 [billion] is not gonna to happen. You may have guessed that, but a reconciliation bill is still possible. It’s going to have to be skinny down to deal with first and foremost the hole in the defense budget that Venezuela and Iran have created,” Rogers, a House defense hawk, said.

Rogers, who will not seek a waiver to remain top Republican on HASC next year, said if the Trump administration can slim down the request from $350 billion down to “100 [billion] or somewhere in that nature, there is a path for that.” 

With doing that, it would be easier to move over the “essential” programs from the reconciliation portion into the baseline Pentagon budget request, which is set at $1.15 trillion, Rogers said. 

The comments come as President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have been pressing Congress to push through the $350 billion package, which includes $17 billion for the Golden Dome missile defense system, $47 billion for expanded munitions production and $48 billion for critical minerals. 

A week ago, the president publicly called on the Senate to pass the reconciliation funding as the time runs out for the Republican majority in Congress. 

“I rebuilt our Military in my First Term, and we’re doing it AGAIN, bigger and better than ever before! The Radical Democrat Majority in the next Congress has already made it clear that their Number One Agenda is to BLOCK and RESIST this historic investment in our National Security,” Trump wrote.

Republican senators have warned that the president’s push for GOP leaders to rely on budget reconciliation process to ram through $350 billion in Pentagon funding could risk a government shutdown, The Hill previously reported. The looming deadline to keep the government open is Dec. 11.  

The Pentagon has continued to call on Capitol Hill to greenlight the request, arguing it is paramount for strengthening the military and safeguarding U.S. national security. 

Pentagon Deputy Secretary Steve Feinberg was at the Senate GOP lunch on Wednesday, according to one GOP source. He discussed the $350 billion request, according to two other sources familiar with the matter. 

Later in the day, he huddled with senators in the Senate Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility (SCIF) to continue those discussions. But the effort has not brought a breakthrough. 

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) described the internal discussion as a  “jump-ball.” 

“Everybody recognizes it’s going to be a Herculean effort to get the House and the Senate in terms of the scope and the process,” Cornyn told reporters after leaving the meeting. 

Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) said the conversations are ongoing, but noted he is for moving the $350 billion package.

“Probably not this week, but again, we are not taking it off the table at all,” Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wisc.) told reporters when asked about reconciliation plans. 

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said earlier this morning he aims to make a decision on if Republicans will move forward with a time-consuming budget reconciliation to fund the Pentagon after the GOP’s Wednesday lunch meeting.

data.title: Trump officials seek to ease anxiety over sweeping tech outages
data.description:
The Trump administration is seeking to calm Americans about a series of tech outages that have raised public anxiety and spurred questions about whether there is a larger problem. 

National Security Advisor Marco Rubio, speaking on camera from Asia, said outages affecting banks, Microsoft and air flights were not connected, a position also backed by Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.), the vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee. This point was reiterated by Homeland Security Sec. Markwayne Mullin and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton at a worldwide threats hearing in the House.

And in an interview at The Hill’s “Red, Flight, and Blue” aviation event, Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford sought to reassure Americans that the country’s aviation system is safe following last week’s outage. 

“The system is absolutely safe,” Bedford said. “The system is old, it’s unstable, but we do have layers and layers of redundancy built into the system to ensure that it flies safely.”

It was unclear whether the administration’s efforts would be successful at quelling speculation about the outages spread on social media. The administration at times has struggled with messaging on the issue since flights were grounded for more than four hours on Friday. Vice President Vance on Wednesday canceled a scheduled appearance at a New York Times Dealbook summit.  

“So far, they’ve had a number of different messengers saying slightly different things,” said Brendan Steinhauser, a Republican strategist and president of the advocacy group Alliance for Secure AI. 

“It’s created some confusion and made people think about whether they have a handle on the situation,” he added. 

Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt echoed this point on Fox News on Tuesday, calling for the White House to prioritize transparency. 

Shortly after Leavitt’s remarks, Clayton began making the rounds on television in an effort to reassure Americans — and the markets. 

“This is not a cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation state. We’ve looked very closely,” Clayton said in an interview on CNBC, before going on Fox Business with a similar message. 

On Capitol Hill on Wednesday, Deputy FBI Director Christopher Raia testified that there was no indication of “cyber malicious activity” in the outages, 

Trump brushed off concerns about the outages when asked by reporters earlier this week, saying “that’s life.” 

But some Trump allies are not convinced by the administration’s answers. Americans also saw outages with Microsoft last week, trouble with financial institutions like J.P. Morgan-Chase on Monday and Apple on Tuesday.

“The American people can see everything happening with these service outages, and they feel like they’re not getting the whole story. You can’t blame anybody for that. I’m a member of Congress, and I feel that way!” Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) wrote in a post on X on Tuesday, calling for congressional briefings on the matter. 

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) called for more answers about the outages while speaking with reporters on Tuesday, openly questioning whether they were a coincidence.

“If this is all a coincidence, it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world,” Hawley said. 

Mullin has come under particular criticism for his response to the FAA ground stop and other tech outages. 

“No offense to Markwayne Mullin, but he seems like an idiot. I just, I have zero faith in this man,” conservative commentator Megyn Kelly said Tuesday on her show. 

“This is a very serious agency, one in which I would like to have some faith in the person heading it up,” she added. 

Mullin also faced heat for taking a government-issued plane to a college football game over the weekend as airports and thousands of passengers were still grappling with the fallout of the ground stop.

At the House hearing, he argued that if he canceled his plans, “it could bring confusion because I was meeting the governor there.”

“I was meeting other people there that would show maybe distrust, that we’re not even willing to fly,” Mullin said. 

Far-right influencer Laura Loomer slammed Mullin’s hearing performance on Capitol Hill Wednesday.

“He should resign,” she wrote. “His performance on The Hill this morning was embarrassing.” 

Some observers say the administration needs to prioritize transparency and consistently communicate the same message. 

Tricia McLaughlin, a former spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, wrote on X Tuesday, “Americans aren’t stupid. We want and deserve to know what’s really going on.”

“Someone high in the administration needs to get on tv and tell the American people NOW what is going on,” Meghan McCain, former Sen. John McCain’s (R-Ariz.) daughter, wrote on X. “No one who lived through Covid is believing this is all a coincidence.” 

The outages also took place amid reporting that Iran has plans to plant a dirty bomb in Washington, DC in an effort to target the highest levels of the administration. 

“We want to be careful not to speculate too much, but I do think given the timing and given the news reporting of the Iranians making plans to decapitate American leadership, I think we all wonder about whether this is part of a broader cyber warfare campaign against the U.S. government and our critical infrastructure,” Steinhauser said. 

However, a White House official said on Wednesday that they are confident the incidents were due to upgrades of legacy computer systems being patched and new hardware being applied. 

“And if you look across the incidents that are being discussed publicly, you can see that the companies that have them, the entities that have them, are disclosing the reasons for them, and that those reasons are disparate, but all are in the upgrading and patching realm,” the official said. 

Tech policy analyst Annie Chestnut Tutor noted the accumulation of outages over a few days has made the situation unique. 

“Unplanned outages due to human error or technical failure could reasonably explain any of these outages, but the accumulation of a global Microsoft outage, a nationwide ground stop, banks, global retailers, airlines, and NSA net being down, that’s highly coincidental,” Tutor said. 

Republican strategist Doug Heye said the responses should always start with facts.

“It starts with facts over speculation. Tell people what you’re doing, without being afraid of saying you don’t know something and are working on getting the answer,” he said. “And when hundreds of people are stranded, you might want to skip the football game.”

— Miranda Nazzaro contributed

data.title: Federal judge extends block on Trump arch construction
data.description:
A federal judge extended an order on Wednesday blocking the Trump administration from moving forward with construction of a 250-foot triumphal arch in the nation’s capital through at least the first week of December.

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan, an Obama appointee who sits on the federal bench in D.C., is now weighing whether to issue a longer-lasting injunction after she handed down a temporary restraining order on Nov. 5 that barred the National Park Service from doing construction on President Trump’s proposed monument.

That order was set to expire on Thursday, but Chutkan said it will remain in effect until at least Dec. 3 to maintain the status quo while litigation continues.

A group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian, as well as the D.C. city government and the state of Virginia, filed separate lawsuits this year seeking to prevent construction of the massive arch — planned for Memorial Circle, a space between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

Chutkan issued her initial order shortly after the National Capital Planning Commission voted to approve the plan, which critics argue is merely a vanity project for the president that would impact airspace and worsen traffic congestion, among other concerns.

The Trump administration contends it has authority to build the arch under a 1925 statute that authorized the Arlington Memorial Bridge Commission to make changes to the bridge which “in its discretion may be found to be necessary or advisable.”

The Justice Department has also leaned on a familiar national security rationale to justify the project, suggesting it would be outfitted with anti-drone technology and serve other purposes vital to national defense.

Chutkan’s extension comes as a federal judge in Virginia is set to hear arguments on Friday in a separate lawsuit brought by the Arlington County Board also seeking a pause in construction.

data.title: Johnson predicts Jeffries will struggle to keep Democrats together in majority
data.description:
Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who was nominated earlier Wednesday to serve as Speaker next term, will have a “hard time” keeping the Democrats together.

“He’s going to have a hard time keeping his conference together, that’s my prediction,” Johnson told a TMZ DC reporter.

When the reporter asked if he thinks Jefferies will do a good job, Johnson responded by saying, “Of course. Hakeem’s a friend, colleague. The American people need Congress to work. I just think it’s going to be a great challenge for him to do that.”

On Wednesday, House Democrats overwhelmingly nominated Jeffries in a 251-11 vote to be the next House Speaker. This is the first step in a two-step process which will be completed with a full House vote on Jan. 3.

The New York Democrat, who ran uncontested, will need 218 votes on the chamber floor in January to secure his position. If he succeeds in getting the required number of votes, Jeffries will be the first Black Speaker in U.S. history.

While Jeffries managed to get a majority of the support from his party, there were some who did not back him.

A group of seven incoming House Democrats, who were among the 11 who voted against Jeffries, issued a joint statement to let their votes be known to the public. The group includes Rep.-elects Darializa Avila Chevalier (N.Y.), Adam Hamawy (N.J.), Frederick Haynes (Texas), Melat Kiros (Colo.), Donavan McKinney (Mich.), Chris Rabb (Pa.) and Claire Valdez (N.Y.).

“We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations. While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership. Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no,” the statement read.

A spokesperson for Haynes said in a statement shared with Time that he “woke up unexpectedly ill this morning” and “narrowly missed the vote.” His team noted that if he did cast his vote, it would have been against Jeffries becoming House Speaker.

data.title: Mullin, Clayton face bipartisan grilling over tech outages
data.description:
Homeland Security Sec. Markwayne Mullin and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said there was no evidence that tech outages hitting businesses across the country were the result of nefarious actions at a timely hearing Wednesday on worldwide threats facing the country.

The series of tech disruptions, including communications failures that led to a Friday groundstop from the Federal Aviation Association (FAA), have fueled questions from the public about whether there is reason for worry.

Fears have also been sparked by reports that Iran is developing plans to set off a dirty bomb in Washington.

Clayton said he understood why people were worried, and why it was raising questions.

“The American people should ask us these questions,” he told the House Homeland Security Committee. “But based on what we know today, after a great deal of diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes.”

“They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack,” Clayton said.

That answer was not fully satisfying to several Republicans as well as Democrats who expressed skepticism there was not a connection linking the various incidents.

“I’m getting a lot of text messages, phone calls about these issues, and I think one of the concerns is how quickly and how many of these outages we’ve seen …in a span of five days, when we’ve never seen that,” said Rep. Eli Crane (R-Ariz.).

Rep. Nick LaLota (R-NY) asked Clayton if he believes in coincidences.

“I believe in exploring coincidences,” Clayton responded.

It was, LaLota acknowledged, a “good answer,” even as the lawmaker said he’s still worried.

“I’m a little worried that what’s happened this last week are a little beyond coincidences,” he stated.

“Thursday, Microsoft 365 went down. Friday, a nationwide ground stop. Monday, United Airlines grounded flights. Also Monday, Chase and Wells Fargo experienced banking disruptions. And yesterday, we learned of a network disruption at the NSA. Five major disruptions in less than a week. Five different explanations,” he said, later asking Clayton if his “gut” tells him its still a coincidence.

“It does, and let me tell you why,” Clayton responded. “It’s an informed opinion, and the reason it’s informed is we are engaged in a substantial increase in upgrades, the number of patches, the number of upgrades that we’re undertaking in the public and private,” Clayton said before explaining the review done by the government.

“We call it red teaming. We say, okay, let’s say we wanted to do this and not be detected, and make it look like it wasn’t coordinated, and try to establish all of that. That’s the kind of exercise that our experts at the FBI and the like will go on,” he said.

Democrats were quick to highlight Trump’s response.

Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-Miss.), the top Democrat on the panel, held up a sign with a quote from Trump, who when asked about the groundstop, said “I don’t take any responsibility.”

Many Democrats cited the gutting of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), which faced widespread firings under Trump and plays a critical role in battling tech vulnerabilities. 

“All three of your agencies – perhaps not Mr. Clayton – have decimated the cybersecurity personnel that this administration entered office with, CISA is way down because the president didn’t want election fraud to be uncovered. The FBI has fired numerous cybersecurity agents because they may or may not have served a subpoena in the Mar-a-Lago case. You all have an obligation to restore that,” said Rep. Dan Goldman (D-N.Y.).

Rep. James Wakinshaw (D-Va.) noted that CISA had 3,400 employees at the start of the Trump administration and pointed to June testimony from Mullin saying the agency was down to 2,200 employees but really needed 2,800.

“Let’s be clear about what happened. The Trump administration inherited a CISA workforce of 3,400 people. They fired and pushed out – more than 1000 cyber defenders – at precisely the moment the cyber threat was exploding. You came before us and said correctly that you needed hundreds of those employees back,” Wakinshaw said.

“So I have a simple question for you: Was it a mistake in 2025 for those employees, the 1,000 plus CISA employees that you now need back? Was it a mistake for them to have been fired and pushed out?”

Mullin wouldn’t say that it was, saying that happened before his arrival.

“I didn’t say [we needed] those employees back. I said we’re hiring new people,” he countered.

The focus on cyber issues overshadowed other major developments that represent potential threats to the nation.

There were just a handful of questions about Iran’s plans for a “dirty bomb.”

Mullin said he did not believe Iran’s exploration of such a weapon constituted an imminent threat.

Clayton wouldn’t get into specifics but did repeatedly highlight the risk posed by Iran in his opening remarks and responses to questions.

“We do face a heightened threat from the Iranians – lethal plotting against our citizens at home and abroad,” he said.

FBI Director Kash Patel skipped the hearing and sent his deputy, bucking a decadelong tradition and garnering a stern rebuke from House Homeland Security Chair Andrew Garbarino (R-N.Y.).

Patel was roasted in absentia by members of both parties for his failure to appear.

“Today’s hearing date was first provided to Director Patel in August. There was no surprise or last-minute request, and despite repeated attempts over the span of several months between then and now to find any date when he could testify, the director made clear that he had no intention of appearing,” Garbarino said in his opening remarks. 

“Director Patel’s refusal to testify marks a significant departure from well-established committee precedent.”

An FBI official said Patel was traveling to field offices this week.

data.title: Pennsylvania reports eighth measles-related death
data.description:
Pennsylvania health officials and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on Wednesday reported the commonwealth’s eighth measles-related death this year, one day after the U.S. lost its measles elimination status after 25 years.

The state’s Department of Health said an unvaccinated Clinton County resident initially tested positive for the virus before their death.

Pennsylvania has seen 1,589 confirmed measles cases across 46 counties, with 28 confirmed cases as of Monday and 315 hospitalizations.

“Getting vaccinated remains the best protection against the measles virus; the vaccine is 97 percent effective at preventing measles for life after two doses,” the department said in a statement.

The Keystone State accounts for more than 1 in 4 cases reported in the entire country, according to the state’s dashboard.

Measles has made a resurgence as vaccination rates have declined. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) had been locked in a bitter dispute with Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a long-time vaccine skeptic, and accused him of “spreading misinformation.” Kennedy said there was no evidence of that.

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) announced on Tuesday that measles was endemic in the U.S., Mexico and Bolivia following a three-day meeting with officials from all three countries. Countries that lose the elimination status must submit a corrective action plan to PAHO in order to regain the status.

Officials with the Trump administration have sought to downplay the significance of losing measles elimination status. Kennedy assured that the outbreak will be stopped and said the COVID-19 pandemic “disrupted” childhood immunizations.

CDC Director Erica Schwartz said that losing the elimination status will not change the federal response to the outbreaks, which has been criticized for being tepid. Administration officials have faced calls for a more robust measles vaccination campaign at the national level, but have questioned the safety and efficacy of the vaccine.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) on Monday cast blame at Kennedy and President Trump for the U.S. losing its elimination status.

“The resurgence of this dangerous virus is a direct consequence of the pathological stupidity plaguing this administration,” Schumer said.

Trump in August signed an executive order recommending the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine be split into three separate shots. He claimed without evidence that together the vaccine is “quite lethal.”

data.title: New York presses ICE on winter safety at tent facility for women
data.description:
The state of New York pressed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) about winter safety at a Batavia detention center for women in a letter sent on Tuesday.

New York’s Department of Health (DOH) and Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) wrote to ICE Deputy Director Charles Wall that they were pursuing “information relating to Akima Infrastructure Protection LLC (Akima)’s construction and anticipated operation of a tent detention facility on behalf of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at the Buffalo Service Processing Center (BSPC).”

“To date, DEC and DOH have not received any information or outreach from the federal government or Akima about this facility,” DEC Commissioner Amanda Lefton and DOH Commissioner of Health James McDonald wrote.

“We understand from public reporting, however, that the facility may be used to detain up to 100 women and will employ numerous staff,” the two officials added.

In October, local outlet the Times Union reported that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) was going ahead with an expansion of the Buffalo (Batavia) Service Processing Center.

According to the Times Union, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told Rep. Timothy Kennedy (D-N.Y.) in a September letter that the expansion was occurring.

Mullin also told Kennedy that the expansion at the ICE facility would hold female detainees, the outlet said.

“We understand that Akima has entered into a contract with ICE and/or DHS to construct and operate a ‘temporary detention structure’ to house up to 100 female detainees of all security levels,” Lefton and McDonald wrote in their letter. “Public contracting documents indicate that the facility will be ‘soft sided’ and will be located adjacent to where the Batavia Service Processing Center is located,”

“The construction and maintenance of a safe and environmentally sound tentbased residential or institutional facility can be difficult. Severe weather, including extended subfreezing temperatures and winter storms, can present additional challenges,” they added.

An ICE spokesperson told The Hill on Wednesday that “It should not come as news that ICE will be making arrests in states across the U.S. and is actively working to expand detention space.”

The Hill has reached out to Akima for comment.

data.title: NIH to move remaining retired research chimps to sanctuary
data.description:
The National Institutes of Health (NIH) announced Wednesday it will release the last government-owned research chimpanzees in early 2027 to a sanctuary, ending a decade-long effort to get the animals out of federal laboratories.

The 34 chimpanzees, currently housed at the Keeling Center for Comparative Medicine and Research in Bastrop, Texas, will be transferred to Chimp Haven, a 200-acre Louisiana sanctuary that serves as the official retirement home for the government-owned apes, the NIH said.

“Completing their transfers will fulfill NIH’s commitment, announced in November 2015, to retire all NIH-owned chimpanzees to sanctuary,” NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya said in a statement.

Bhattacharya added the timing of the transfers, which are expected to begin early next year, will be “guided by the chimpanzees’ health, welfare and social groupings.”

The agency announced in 2015 it would no longer conduct or fund invasive research involving chimpanzees following outrage from animal rights activists calling to protect the endangered species. 

Chimps were used historically for biomedical research on diseases such as HIV, hepatitis and cancer due to their biological similarities to humans. Scientists used the primates to study viruses and test the safety of medical treatments — including pharmaceutical drugs and radiation — until the NIH suspended funding for the practice in 2011.

The agency then pledged to retire all government-owned animals to sanctuaries, citing an independent assessment of the usefulness of chimpanzees for biomedical research and the designation of all chimps as endangered under the Endangered Species Act in 2015.

“We find no evidence that there is a need to continue to do research of an invasive sort on chimpanzees, not now and not going to in the future,” then-NIH Director Francis S. Collins said at the time.

Since then, more than 200 chimpanzees have been relocated to Chimp Haven in Keithville, Louisiana. At Chimp Haven, the animals live in large, forested areas and social groups designed to resemble their natural habitats.

“This has been a long road and something that many people thought would never happen,” Kathleen Conlee, vice president of animal research issues at Humane World for Animals, said in a statement to The New York Times. “It’s a really historic moment. This will be the end of the government’s use and confinement of chimps in labs.”
